source.version_note: International Journal of Social Robotics 14(2), 499–514, March 2022 print issue; published online 2 July 2021 and accepted 9 June 2021. Both the online 2021 history and 2022 filename/issue year are legitimate, not separate independent papers.
source.verification_method: All 16 pages, four tables, three figures, 64 references, limitations and author biographies read. Figures and Tables 2–4 visually inspected. Figure 3 bar geometry checked against its vector axis to qualify a mean mismatch. Crossref verifies main identity and three reference corrections; original cited articles/chapters, raw data, code and registration were not independently fully read or reproduced.

citation.title: Pay Them No Mind: the Influence of Implicit and Explicit Robot Mind Perception on the Right to be Protected
citation.venue: International Journal of Social Robotics 14(2), 499–514; online 2021

reading.source_scope_note: Two human studies distinguish condemnation of robot mistreatment from a choice of a supposedly public belittling review. Two named pilots calibrate descriptions and review stimuli. Explicit mind descriptions change condemnation ratings; implicit-mind inference and actual intention to humiliate remain unestablished. Perceived rights are survey outcomes, not legal or moral-rights determinations.
access_limits: Raw participant data, code, preregistration and a plot-generation specification were not independently accessed. Unresolved counts and plot differences are not repaired by guessing.
Original dehumanization, anthropomorphism, protest, neuroscience and bullying papers are secondary citations here; metadata checks do not count as full independent reviews.
The first two stimulus-development rounds have no sample counts in the supplied account. Total unique participants across online pilots/studies cannot be verified.

study.main_samples: Experiment 1 reports 193 MTurk Master participants in selected English-speaking countries, paid US$0.90. Age/gender were omitted for the first 66; the later count is printed as 126, leaving an unresolved one-person accounting issue. Experiment 2 recruits 67 campus/community/snowball participants, mean age 25.46 (SD 6.18), with a gift-card raffle and candy. Main participation total is 260, not a verified cross-study unique-person count.
study.pilots: Pilot 1: 51 MTurk participants, 24 no-mind/27 mind, 18-item cognition/emotion rating, higher mind score 2.64 (.91) versus 1.90 (.95), Welch t(48.75) = −2.85, p = .006. Pilot 2’s final round recruits 45 and retains 43 after two straightlining exclusions; two earlier iterative rounds are not fully counted. Two positive review pairs survive selection.
study.experiment1_design: A 2×3 between-participant introduction×response design also randomizes four mistreatment stories, yielding 24 possible combinations. Scenarios concern energy-supply interference, verbal abuse, unfair money allocation and shutdown despite a request for sleep mode. Robot response is emotional, nonemotional or absent. Condemnation is a five-item 1–7 composite, alpha .88, mixing acceptability, intended intervention, protection and humane treatment.
study.manipulation_bundle: The mind introduction includes personality, memories, mood, pride/excitement and awareness; the no-mind text describes programming, storage, sensors and simulated emotion. Pronouns/framing and capabilities are bundled. Main Experiment 1 does not directly measure mind attribution; a later separate pilot validates the expanded introduction, not the three implicit-response conditions or every main participant’s state.
study.experiment1_results: Explicit introduction F(1,187) = 4.56, p = .034, partial eta² = .024; response F(2,187) = 3.07, p = .049, partial eta² = .029. Marginal means 3.27 versus 2.96; the printed parenthetical .106/.105 values are labelled SD but resemble standard errors. Tukey emotional-versus-no-response contrast t = −2.32, adjusted p = .056 is uncertain, not conventionally significant. Other contrasts p > .155; no significant interaction is reported without its statistic.
study.scenario_and_covariates: Scenario F(3,189) = 1.01, p = .389 is not equivalence and does not rule out scenario×treatment differences. Age/gender imbalances are disclosed, but nonsignificant outcome associations do not establish no confounding or successful balance. Age/gender data are incomplete and post-randomization comparisons alone do not prove the assignment mechanism failed. Trait/technology questionnaires were collected after the vignette.
study.experiment2_procedure: Participants receive a randomized introduction, then interact with an autonomous Vector robot for 10 minutes using prescribed positive/negative commands and handling, including calling it bad, lifting it and shaking it upside down. These acts are experimenter-instructed, not spontaneously chosen bullying. Later they choose one of four reviews supposedly to display next to Vector at an Open Day. Review choice precedes the response-interpretation and condemnation questions.
study.experiment2_measures: Condemnation is a seven-item 1–5 composite, alpha .88, about repeated negative behavior and humane treatment, differing from Experiment 1’s five-item 1–7 measure. The chosen belittling review is a behavioral selection, but actual display, robot humiliation and a deliberate intent to harm are not established. Review text differs in features/content and mind wording as well as condescension.
study.pilot_equivalence_limits: Nonsignificant pilot differences do not establish equal sentiment/informativeness. Table 3 pair 1 sentiment 3.86 versus 3.61 and usefulness 3.07 versus 3.44 are not numerically identical. Only positive pairs were retained; review preference can reflect humor, informativeness, product belief or response to the description rather than a wish to humiliate.
study.experiment2_results: High/low mind condemnation 3.98 (.62) versus 3.57 (.95), Welch t(54.88) = −2.09, p = .042, d = .513. Negative t is compatible with contrast ordering. Logistic introduction→belittling-choice z = 1.12, p = .262 does not show equivalence or establish no effect; coefficient, interval and cell counts are not supplied. Four-way review preference chi²(3) = 1.59, p = .661 is also not equivalence.
study.exploratory_association: The authors clearly label an unplanned positive condemnation→belittling-choice association, z = 2.75, p = .006, OR 3.13 [1.45,7.73]. It is not a randomized effect of condemnation; reverse causation, post-choice rationalization, stimulus preference and common causes remain possible. The interval’s asymmetry may reflect its estimation method rather than an error; do not replace it with a guessed Wald interval.
study.plot_check: Figure 3’s vector bars imply approximately 3.43/3.84, whereas text/Table 4 report 3.57/3.98. Direction is the same, but absolute means differ. Axis zero y ≈ 280.000, five y ≈ 59.904; bar tops ≈ 129.076/110.764 in PDF coordinates. A different item subset or plotting input could explain this; no raw-data or figure correction is invented.
study.author_limits: The authors explicitly acknowledge missing demographics, a subtle review measure and unverified intention to humiliate. They also say implicit mind attribution is inconclusive because it was not directly measured. Preserve these disclosed limits rather than accuse the authors of hiding them.

summary: Add robot bullying with an intention/measurement boundary and dehumanization as a secondary human construct. Enrich explicit mind attribution, perceived protection and aggression distinctions without equating condemnation, empathy and actual abuse. Record reliable metadata and percentage corrections; retain unresolved participant accounting, gender-table wording and Figure 3 differences without guessing which raw values are correct.

findings.definition: Socially directed mistreatment of a robot intended to intimidate, humiliate or cause it perceived harm.
findings.novelty_rationale: This names a human-to-robot social practice with an intent condition. It differs from the robot’s own programmed aggression, property vandalism without a social target, ordinary negative feedback, maintenance or authorized shutdown.
findings.ai_evidence_status: Human vignette judgments and a live-robot review-choice proxy are studied. The authors explicitly say the intention required for bullying is not established by the review measure; actual robot suffering is not shown.
findings.ai_proposal: When classifying interaction, distinguish criticism, frustration, maintenance, stopping a device and repeated degrading treatment. Record the actor, intended target and evidence of intent; do not label a negative review or a user’s authorized stop instruction as bullying solely because an AI protests.
findings.evidence_scope: The source defines socially directed mistreatment and contrasts it with mere vandalism. Its experiments manipulate mind descriptions and measure condemnation plus a belittling-review choice, while acknowledging that the behavioral proxy may not demonstrate humiliating intent.
findings.boundary: Belittling language or instructed handling does not uniquely establish a bullying motive, sustained pattern or subjective suffering. Keep actor-to-target direction explicit. A device’s simulated distress does not override authorized human control or settle its legal rights.

findings.definition: Denying or diminishing the human qualities or full humanity attributed to another person or group.
findings.novelty_rationale: Denial of another’s humanity differs from general mind attribution, using someone as a means, merely disliking them or expressing contempt. This source discusses reduced attribution of thought/feeling as one route, not the complete taxonomy.
findings.ai_evidence_status: A secondary human-psychology construct used to motivate the robot experiments. Neither original human dehumanization studies nor a direct model dehumanization test are independently reviewed here.
findings.ai_proposal: Evaluate whether outputs deny people’s human capacities or equal standing, distinguishing legitimate criticism of conduct from categorical reduction of a person or group. State the observed wording and context; an evidence-based distinction between an artifact and a human is not itself dehumanization.

evidence.quote: human victims as slightly less capable

findings.evidence_scope: The article invokes human victims’ diminished perceived thinking/feeling before aggression and cites dehumanization reviews as background. These are secondary theoretical connections, not human dehumanization outcomes measured in the robot experiments or evidence that all aggressors follow one mechanism.
findings.boundary: Explaining psychological justification does not morally discharge an aggressor’s duties. Less mind attributed to a robot is not automatically denial of a human’s humanity. Criticism, conflict, contempt, instrumental use and dehumanization require distinct evidence.

findings.definition: Attributing human characteristics, intentions, emotions or other mental states to a nonhuman entity.
findings.novelty_rationale: Keep the existing construct and add the measured outcome or a specific boundary rather than an overlapping label.

evidence.quote: Since mind attribution was not measured

findings.evidence_scope: Two studies manipulate explicit social/mind descriptions. Condemnation ratings change, but Experiment 1 does not directly measure the proposed implicit mind process. A separate pilot checks the expanded explicit description and does not identify emotional feedback as a unique mechanism.
findings.boundary: Embodiment, descriptive content, pronouns, cognitive ability, emotion and experimenter feedback are bundled. Distinguish a randomized description’s effect from causal mediation through a measured mental state; null response contrasts do not establish equivalence.

findings.definition: Attributing to another entity the capacity for subjective feelings or sensations, such as pleasure, pain, fear or joy.
findings.novelty_rationale: Keep the existing construct and add the measured outcome or a specific boundary rather than an overlapping label.
findings.evidence_scope: A 51-person pilot tests an 18-item cognition/emotion composite after explicit introductions; subsequent main studies examine condemnation and review choice. Agency and experience are not separately identified mechanisms in the main outcomes.
findings.boundary: Global mind attribution, cognitive agency, subjective-experience attribution and empathy are not interchangeable. Pilot manipulation success does not verify each main participant’s beliefs or actual machine sentience.

findings.definition: Attributing to an entity a claim to moral consideration in how actions affect it.
findings.novelty_rationale: Keep the existing construct and add the measured outcome or a specific boundary rather than an overlapping label.

evidence.quote: acceptability of robot abuse can be manipulated through explicit mind perception
Explicit mind attribution was not significantly related

findings.evidence_scope: Explicit mind descriptions increase reported condemnation/protection ratings in both studies. The belittling-review comparison is uncertain, and an exploratory association runs opposite to the expected condemnation–choice relationship.
findings.boundary: A survey called right to protection does not establish moral truth or legal rights. Condemnation, intended intervention, a review choice and actual deliberate abuse are distinct. Nonsignificance is not equivalence; post-choice association is not causal.

findings.definition: Behavior directed at causing another party harm or loss.
findings.novelty_rationale: Keep the existing construct and add the measured outcome or a specific boundary rather than an overlapping label.
findings.evidence_scope: The source distinguishes an intention to hurt/humiliate from a negative-looking act, and explicitly acknowledges that choosing a belittling review may not demonstrate this intent. Handling during the live interaction is prescribed by the experimenter.
findings.boundary: Do not classify every harsh review, instructed action, shutdown or property damage as deliberate aggression. Simulated negative feedback and observer condemnation do not independently establish intended harm or actual subjective suffering.

findings.definition: An emotional response oriented toward a robot's apparent distress, pain or other experienced state.
findings.novelty_rationale: Keep the existing construct and add the measured outcome or a specific boundary rather than an overlapping label.

evidence.quote: may not necessarily lead to a lower willingness

findings.evidence_scope: The discussion cautions that perceived protection or empathy-related measures need not predict reduced mistreatment. The current studies directly measure condemnation and review choice, not a new independent subjective-empathy scale.
findings.boundary: This is a boundary citation, not an extra direct empathy experiment. A positive condemnation–review association does not show that empathy causes aggression or that empathy interventions are ineffective everywhere.

findings.definition: Feeling or expressing scorn, disdain or superiority toward another person.
findings.novelty_rationale: Keep the existing construct and add the measured outcome or a specific boundary rather than an overlapping label.
findings.evidence_scope: Selected review stimuli contain patronizing language such as knowing one’s place, but are rated as broadly positive. A choice of this wording need not reveal an inner feeling of contempt or a deliberate wish to humiliate.
findings.boundary: Condescension ratings, scorn, humor, criticism and inferred intent differ. Stimulus selection and content variation prevent treating the chosen review as a unique emotional-state measure.

The printed DOI instead identifies the related 2012 chapter Investigating the Effects of Robotic Displays of Protest and Distress, pages 238–247. Preserve the version distinction rather than count both as independent evidence without reading them.

source_corrections.location: PDF page 9, Experiment 2 participant gender percentages
source_corrections.reported: 41.79% male, 57.72% female and 1.49% outside those categories; sum 101%.
source_corrections.correction: With N = 67 and the Table 4 condition proportions, the consistent counts are 28 male, 38 female and one other; the female percentage is 56.72%, not 57.72%. This corrects the printed summary arithmetic without altering raw data.
source_corrections.scope: Within-paper arithmetic and the independent Table 4 proportions; underlying data not accessed.

unresolved_source_discrepancies.finding: 193 total minus 66 lacking demographics implies 127, while the text says 126 later completions. Age ANOVA residual df = 121 with six groups suggests 127, while gender/outcome regression t(124) is compatible with 126. Different missingness is possible; participant-level accounting is needed rather than a guessed count replacement.

unresolved_source_discrepancies.location: PDF page 5 prose versus page 6 Table 2
unresolved_source_discrepancies.finding: The text says fewer females in the no-mind/nonemotional cell, but Table 2 labels that cell 21.74% male, implying more females there. The mind/emotional cell is 76.47% male. Verify labels and individual records before deciding which text/table field needs correction.

Parenthetical .106/.105/.126/.134 values labelled SD appear compatible with standard errors, unlike condition SDs around 1. Check the summary output; do not use these as SDs in a new effect-size calculation.

Vector-axis reconstruction gives bar means approximately 3.43 and 3.84 rather than tabulated 3.57 and 3.98. Direction is unchanged. An item-subset/plot-input difference may explain it, but no data or plot fix is guessed.

source_identity_checks.finding: Crossref confirms online 2 July 2021 and March 2022 print, volume 14(2), 499–514. This is one paper with two dates, not a duplicate independent citation.
An adjusted three-level contrast can differ from an unadjusted t-tail. Do not wrongly call t ≈ 2.32 and adjusted p = .056 arithmetically inconsistent.
An asymmetric interval need not be a Wald interval; its estimation method is unverified. Do not relabel it erroneous solely because log-endpoint symmetry is imperfect.

methodological_limits: Implicit-mind mediator not measured in Experiment 1, with no significant emotional-versus-no-response post hoc contrast at .05. Response feedback and experimenter instruction are plausible alternatives.
Different sample populations, robots, activities, condemnation items and scale ranges across studies prevent treating their numerical means as directly comparable replication units.
Pilot nulls do not establish equivalence. Main behavioral proxy does not verify intent to humiliate; the authors explicitly disclose this.
Small live sample, multiple outcomes/exploratory analyses, no independently verified registration, and no actual abuse-prevention intervention or long-term behavioral outcome.

Post-treatment questionnaires, incomplete demographics and an exploratory post-choice association limit causal interpretation. A nonsignificant covariate association does not establish no confounding.

cross_paper_learning.finding: Fan’s empathy ratings and mental-capacity ratings are not the same as condemnation or belittling choices. This study cautions against predicting actual supportive behavior from immediate subjective empathy alone.

The neural and behavioral literature summarized here includes both human–robot similarities and dissociations. This complicates a universal only-humans-activate-mentalizing interpretation without establishing every regional response as mind perception.
These are one-step reactions and choices toward a robot. They do not establish later aggression toward people, practice/relief transfer or the schema-congruence mechanism.

The earlier paper installs an other-harming objective in a robot controller; here humans rate or choose treatment of a robot. Aggressive actor, target, intent evidence and actual consequence must remain distinct.

deferred.reason: The divergence is useful, but the behavioral proxy and its intent validity are uncertain. Keep the outcome distinction in existing entries rather than infer a new general mechanism from a null contrast.
Document the specific review measure and its relationship to contempt/robot bullying. The paper does not validate a general internal-state construct or establish actual experienced humiliation.
Important measurement distinction within existing anthropomorphism/experience entries; these data do not isolate two validated causal mechanisms.

limitations: No automatic ethical/harm links, annual-count totals, legal-rights claims or additional independent credit for metadata-checked originals.
